what_its_for: Valbenazine is used to treat tardive dyskinesia (TD). Tardive dyskinesia causes uncontrolled, repetitive movements of the face, tongue, lips, or other parts of the body. These movements can happen as a side effect of certain psychiatric medications. Valbenazine helps reduce these involuntary movements so you can feel more comfortable and in control.
how_to_take: Take valbenazine by mouth once a day. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the capsule whole — do not open, crush, or chew it. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. If you have trouble swallowing the capsule, talk to your pharmacist or doctor before changing how you take it.
dosing: Your doctor will usually start you on a lower dose (40 mg once daily) and may increase it to 80 mg once daily after one week, depending on how well you respond and how you tolerate the medication. Some patients may stay on 40 mg if the higher dose causes side effects. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next regular dose at your usual time. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store valbenazine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medication after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking valbenazine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Be careful when driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require alertness until you know how this medication affects you. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, especially antidepressants, antifungals like ketoconazole, or HIV medications, as some drugs can interact with valbenazine and change how it works.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: a fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat (this could be a sign of a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation); signs of depression, suicidal thoughts, or changes in mood or behavior; severe drowsiness or trouble staying awake; fainting or dizziness; or if your uncontrolled movements get worse. Also contact your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or are breastfeeding.
when_it_works: Some patients begin to notice improvement in their uncontrolled movements within the first few weeks of treatment. However, it may take up to 4 to 8 weeks or longer to see the full benefit. Be patient and keep taking your medication as directed, even if you do not notice changes right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like drowsiness and dizziness, so use caution. If you have liver problems, your doctor may prescribe a lower dose because the medication stays in your body longer. Valbenazine is not approved for use in children. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before taking this medication, as the effects on unborn babies and nursing infants are not fully known.
